Collectively, these findings demonstrate that C. indica KUFC144 is a rich source of antibacterial metabolites and highlight forsythiaside as a promising GyrB-targeting lead based on the Vina score (predicted binding affinity). At the same time, the ADME analysis provides additional information for prioritizing the identified metabolites. The study provides a foundation for future biochemical validation and the development of mushroom-derived antibacterial agents.

title: Bacterial and fungal pathogens in adult dacryocystitis: a retrospective study from a tertiary medical center in southern Taiwan
abstract: To investigate the microbiological spectrum of dacryocystitis in southern Taiwan, with emphasis on polymicrobial and fungal infections, and to inform treatment based on regional susceptibility patterns. This retrospective study enrolled patients with culture-proven dacryocystitis who underwent lacrimal surgery at a tertiary medical center in southern Taiwan from 2014 to 2024. Routine fungal culture was implemented after July 2018. Only intraoperative specimens obtained under sterile conditions were analyzed to minimize contamination. Among 216 dacryocystitis cases (102 acute and 114 chronic), 179 (82.9%) were culture-positive. Staphylococcus aureus and Cutibacterium acnes were commonly identified in acute cases, whereas Pseudomonas aeruginosa and S. epidermidis were more frequent in chronic cases. After routine fungal culture was implemented, fungi were detected in 19 of 154 cases (12.3%), predominantly in chronic cases. Oxacillin resistance was observed in 13 of 36 S. aureus isolates (36.1%), while most Gram-negative isolates remained susceptible to gentamicin, amikacin, and piperacillin-tazobactam. Our findings demonstrate a diverse microbial spectrum in adult dacryocystitis, including Gram-negative, polymicrobial, and fungal involvement, particularly in chronic disease. The observed antimicrobial resistance patterns suggest that Gram-positive-focused empirical therapy may not provide adequate coverage. Comprehensive microbiological evaluation, including fungal culture, together with consideration of local susceptibility patterns may improve treatment selection, particularly in chronic or refractory dacryocystitis.

title: Fates and Characteristics of Antibiotic Resistance Genes Carried by Viruses during a Full-Scale Anaerobic Sludge Digestion
abstract: The transmission of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) mediated by viruses in sludge represents an emerging concern for antibiotic resistance dissemination. This study investigated the virus-carried ARGs (vARGs) profiles and potential risks in sludges collected from an entire anaerobic sludge digestion plant. A total of 79 unique vARGs spanning 10 antibiotic resistance classes were identified, with trimethoprim resistance genes being the most diverse. Although most vARGs (94.9%) exhibited low sequence similarity (< 70%) to known ARGs, the representative functional validation showed that virus-carried dfr genes could confer trimethoprim resistance to Escherichia coli. Thermal hydrolysis reduced the levels and diversity of vARGs, whereas subsequent anaerobic digestion led to substantial enrichment. More than 90% of vARGs in sludge viromes were removed after all treatment processes, but a significant number of ARG-carrying viruses (10- 10VLPs/g) still remained in the final sludges. In the metagenomes, the levels of vARGs increased approximately 7-fold, suggesting that vARGs were more difficult to be moved than plasmid-associated ARGs and chromosome-associated ARGs. The host prediction suggested associations between some vARG-carrying viruses and potential pathogenic bacteria, which worthing further experimental validation. In summary, the persistence of vARGs in sludge remains a concern, even after the implementation of sludge treatment processes.

title: Repurposing Ionophores to Tackle Antimicrobial Resistance with a Focus on PBT2
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains a growing global health challenge. While resistant bacterial strains continue to emerge and spread, the development of new antibiotics has remained slow. This gap has increased interest in drug repurposing as a promising strategy to combat multidrug-resistant (MDR) pathogens. Ionophores are a structurally diverse group of natural and synthetic compounds that transport ions across biological membranes. Many ionophores were originally developed and widely used for the prevention and treatment of coccidiosis, a common protozoan parasitic intestinal disease in poultry and livestock. Recent studies suggest that some ionophores inhibit bacterial growth directly or enhance the activity of existing antibiotics by perturbing bacterial metal homeostasis, inducing oxidative stress, disturbing membrane function and disrupting biofilms. Among these compounds, PBT2, an 8-hydroxyquinoline derivative with zinc/copper ionophore activity, is an important example. PBT2 acts principally as an antibiotic adjuvant, restoring the activity of conventional antibiotics against several MDR pathogens when combined with zinc. PBT2 also demonstrates narrow-spectrum bactericidal activity as a monotherapy against selected Gram-negative bacteria, including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitidis and Helicobacter pylori. PBT2 has prior human exposure from Phase II trials in neurodegenerative diseases, but its antibacterial pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics remain undefined. This review summarises the discovery, classification and repurposing of ionophores, and examines the antibacterial activities of PBT2 and its proposed mechanisms of action. Finally, we discuss the translational barriers to the clinical use of ionophores, including bacterial selectivity, resistance risk, toxicity and safety.

title: From Individual-Based Models to Macroscopic Dynamics of Antimicrobial Resistance
abstract: We introduce and discuss a kinetic framework describing the time evolution of the statistical distributions of a population divided into the compartments of susceptible, infectious, recovered, and resistant in the presence of a microbial infection driven by susceptible-infectious interactions. Our main objective is to quantify the impact of excessive and inappropriate antimicrobial use, which accelerates the spread of resistance by enabling a fraction of infectious individuals to transition into the resistant compartment. The model consists of a system of Boltzmann-type equations capturing binary interactions between susceptible and infectious individuals, complemented by linear redistribution operators that represent recovery, the development of resistance, and reinfection processes. In the grazing-collision limit, we show that this Boltzmann system is well approximated by a system of coupled Fokker-Planck equations. This limiting description allows for a more tractable analysis of the dynamics, including the characterization of the long-time behavior of the population densities. Our analysis highlights how interaction terms drive the system toward a stable equilibrium and quantifies the effects of inappropriate antimicrobial use on the distribution of resistant individuals. Overall, the results offer a multi-scale perspective that bridges kinetic theory with classical epidemic modeling.

title: Exposure to the Broad-Spectrum Disinfectant Glutaraldehyde Facilitates Antibiotic Resistance Genes Dissemination via Plasmid-Mediated Conjugation
abstract: Plasmid-mediated conjugative transfer is a major driver of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) dissemination, posing serious risks to ecosystems and human health. Glutaraldehyde (GA), a widely used disinfectant, is increasingly detected in environmental matrices, raising emerging concerns regarding its potential to promote ARGs spread. However, whether GA influences plasmid transfer remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that environmentally relevant concentrations of GA (0.01-1 mg/L) significantly enhanced the conjugative transfer of the multidrug resistance plasmid pKJK5 across both intra- and inter-genus bacterial systems. GA increased transfer frequencies by up to 4.29-fold in pure cultures and 4.16-fold in wastewater microbial communities, facilitating ARGs dissemination to diverse taxa, including several opportunistic pathogens. Mechanistically, GA damaged the integrity of the cell membrane , induced ROS production and the SOS response, promoted cell motility and biofilm formation, and upregulated genes involved in ROS detoxification, SOS regulation, membrane permeability, and conjugation. Nontargeted metabolomics profiling and molecular docking further supported these observations. Our findings reveal a previously overlooked role of GA in accelerating ARGs dissemination and underscore the environmental risks posed by commonly used disinfectants in driving the spread of clinically relevant multidrug-resistant pathogens.

title: Three-dimensional microfluidic nanoprecipitation of zein-loaded polyethylene glycol poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles with sustained-release antibacterial activity
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance calls for innovative drug delivery strategies that enhance natural antibacterial agents while minimizing off-target toxicity. Most cationic antimicrobial nanocarriers rely on electrostatic membrane binding as a prerequisite for bactericidal activity, which may compromise biocompatibility through nonspecific interactions with host cells. Here, we propose a nanoparticle-bacterium contact-independent sustained-release antibacterial approach using zein-loaded PEG-PLGA nanoparticles fabricated via three-dimensional (3D) microfluidic nanoprecipitation. The optimized nanoparticles (112.3 ± 7.1 nm, -35.4 ± 4.1 mV, 8.4 ± 1.0% drug loading) exhibited excellent colloidal stability, attenuated burst release, prolonged sustained release, preserved zein's intrinsic antioxidant activity, and supported favorable hemocompatibility and low cytotoxicity. Antibacterial assays revealed significantly enhanced activity against Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) (minimal inhibitory concentration, MIC 1.0 mg/mL, minimum bactericidal concentration, MBC 2.0 mg/mL) and Escherichia coli (E. coli) (MIC 1.5 mg/mL, MBC 3.0 mg/mL) versus free zein. Three independent lines of evidence supported the proposed nanoparticle-bacterium contact-independent sustained-release antibacterial mechanism. Scanning electron microscopy showed dose-dependent bacterial membrane rupture, while zeta potential measurements revealed no change in bacterial surface charge, indicating no detectable electrostatic adsorption. Propidium iodide uptake assays further demonstrated membrane permeabilization of approximately 50% at MIC and over 85% at MBC. Blank nanoparticles caused no membrane damage, suggesting that sustained drug liberation from the non-adherent carrier is a major contributor. This work provides evidence that potent antibacterial activity can occur without detectable electrostatic membrane adsorption under the tested conditions, offering a differentiated design principle for next-generation antibacterial nanomedicines.

title: Aptamer-Functionalized Pro-Photosensitizers for Targeted Elimination of Drug-Resistant Bacterial Biofilm Infection by Sequentially Activated Photodynamic-Antibiotic Therapy
abstract: Drug-resistant bacterial infections seriously threaten public health, and the formation of a biofilm barrier plays an important role. Drug-resistant biofilms are difficult to remove because the penetration and specificity of traditional antimicrobial drugs are poor, and the microenvironment in the inner layer of biofilms is hypoxic. Herein, we developed activatable aptamer-functionalized pro-photosensitizers (APMB) by modifying the clinical photosensitizer methylene blue (MB) with an aptamer that can specifically bind to drug-resistant bacteria. The APMB can simultaneously achieve imaging-guided efficient anti-infection and biofilm destruction, thereby increasing the therapeutic efficiency of the treatment of bacterial biofilm infections. Additionally, we co-loaded APMB and the antibiotic metronidazole (MNZ) into hydrogels to prepare a degradable microneedle patch, which can utilize photodynamic effects to eliminate biofilms under normoxic conditions and potentiate the hypoxic microenvironment to activate the antibacterial activity of MNZ, ultimately resulting in the synergistic killing of deep-seated bacteria. To summarize, this simple and intelligent phototheranostic molecular platform improves deep anti-infection efficacy through the synergistic effect of sequential activation while decreasing systemic toxicity, thereby providing a promising avenue for clinical translation to combat antimicrobial resistance.

title: A Selective Bis-Catecholate Siderophore-Ampicillin Conjugate Expands Activity against Multidrug-Resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a global public health crisis, with multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa among the most critical threats. The high cost and slow pace of novel antibiotic development, coupled with rapid resistance evolution, demand innovative strategies. Here, we present a Trojan horse approach using siderophore-antibiotic conjugates (SACs) to hijack bacterial iron uptake systems and deliver β-lactam payloads across the Gram-negative outer membrane. We designed a series of ampicillin conjugates with mono-catecholate, bis-catecholate, and catecholate-hydroxamate siderophores. These conjugates demonstrate potent antimicrobial activity. Notably, the lead compound, BC-2-Amp, shows broad-spectrum and highly selective activity against a panel of 105 clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that BC-2-Amp utilizes PiuA as a critical receptor for targeted delivery. Complementary in vivo experiments further confirmed its promising therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, these findings establish SACs as a potent strategy for broadening the spectrum of β-lactam antibiotics and provide a robust platform for high-potency drug delivery.

title: Design, Synthesis, and Preliminary Investigation on the Mode of Action for a Series of Novel Antimicrobial Peptidomimetics
abstract: Over the years, many antibiotics have been developed, but most have become less effective due to antimicrobial resistance, especially those targeting enzymatic pathways. This growing resistance poses a serious global health threat. It is now recognized that physically disrupting bacterial cell membranes is less prone to resistance development. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are promising in this regard, though their broader application is limited by their susceptibility to proteolytic degradation and toxicity. To address these issues, peptidomimetics have emerged as a new class of antibacterial agents. In this study, a library of AMPs were designed and synthesized, inspired by magainin, a defensin-mimetic molecule, and brilacidin. Modifying side chain lengths proved essential for effective insertion into phospholipid bilayers. A modular synthetic approach was developed, enabling the generation of diverse derivatives to explore structure-activity relationships. The compounds were tested against clinically relevant pathogens, showing promising antimicrobial activity, and preliminary studies confirmed a membranolytic mechanism of action.

title: Triple Combination Therapy: A Promising Path Forward against β-Lactamase-Mediated Resistance
abstract: The silent pandemic of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to drive global morbidity and mortality. Resistance is often mediated by co-expression of serine β-lactamases (SBLs) and metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), limiting treatment options. While several SBL inhibitors are clinically available, MBL inhibitors are yet to reach the market, and only a few candidates are in late-stage development. Dual-β-lactamase inhibitors remain an unmet goal. To preserve existing antibiotics, alternative strategies are required. This perspective highlights triple combination therapy comprising a β-lactam antibiotic, an SBL inhibitor, and an MBL-targeting agent to achieve broader coverage. Notably, in 2025, the U.S Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved aztreonam-avibactam (Emblaveo), in combination with metronidazole, for adults with complicated intra-abdominal infections who have limited or no alternative treatment options. Expanding such strategies may help mitigate AMR and support ongoing antimicrobial development efforts.

title: Comparative phytochemical and spectroscopic characterization of selected plant extracts and honey with potential antimicrobial application against bovine mastitis
abstract: This study compares the bioactive compounds and phytochemical constituents of,,, and honey fromBovine mastitis remains a major challenge for the global dairy industry, causing substantial economic losses through reduced milk production, increased treatment costs, and premature culling. These challenges have increased interest in alternative plant-based products, including herbal extracts and honey. Among the evaluated samples,showed the highest TFC (77.3 mg QE/g) and TPC (80.9 mg GAE/g). An antimicrobial assay againstfurther demonstrated thatexhibited the strongest antibacterial activity. The presence of major phenolic acids and flavonoids was confirmed by HPLC analysis, whereas GC-MS provided exploratory information on selected volatile and semi-volatile constituents, including fatty acids and terpenoid-related compounds. FTIR analysis further supported the presence of characteristic functional groups associated with the detected phytoconstituents. Overall, the findings support further investigation of these natural materials as potential sources of antimicrobial agents.

title: Correction: Virulence arsenal and antibiotic resistance backgrounds in Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates from hospital wastewater samples from Iraq
Genomic characterization of Fusobacterium necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain JKSFn-26 associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir, India
abstract: Fusobacterium necrophorum is an important anaerobic bacterium associated with the progression and severity of ovine footrot. However, genomic information on footrot associated isolates, particularly those recovered from severe lesions, remains limited. Here, we report the genomic characterization of F. necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain JKSFn-26, isolated from a severe ovine footrot lesion in Kashmir, India. The isolate was characterized phenotypically and assigned to the previously identified JKS-F3 leukotoxin (lktA) variant by partial gene sequence analysis. Whole genome sequencing was performed using the Illumina HiSeq platform. The draft genome was subjected to annotation, phylogenomic analysis, and in silico screening for virulence associated genes, toxin-related determinants, antimicrobial resistance associated genes, and adaptive defense elements. JKSFn-26 belonged to the JKS-F3 lktA variant previously associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir, and the analyzed lktA gene fragment showed 100% nucleotide identity with the reported JKS-F3 sequence. The draft genome was 2.23 Mb with a G + C content of 34.37% and contained 2,048 predicted coding sequences, 45 tRNAs, five rRNAs, four annotated non-coding RNAs, one tmRNA, two CRISPR arrays, and ten pseudogenes. Phylogenomic analysis placed JKSFn-26 within the F. necrophorum subsp. necrophorum clade. The genome contained the lktBAC locus and predicted virulence associated determinants related to hemolytic activity, adhesion, iron acquisition, and outer membrane proteins. Multiple toxin-antitoxin modules and putative antimicrobial resistance associated determinants were also identified. The deduced LktA amino acid sequence showed 98.0% identity to the corresponding leukotoxin A sequence of Fusobacterium necrophorum subsp. necrophorum strain ATCC 25286 . This study provides genomic information on a JKS-F3 lktA variant associated with severe ovine footrot in Kashmir and expands genomic resources for F. necrophorum.

title: Biological characterization of the lytic Pseudomonas aeruginosa phage BUCT980 and its therapeutic efficacy in a murine lung infection model
abstract: is an important opportunistic pathogen whose increasing multidrug resistance limits conventional antimicrobial treatment options and underscores the need for alternative antibacterial strategies. In this study, we isolated and systematically characterized a novel lytic phage, BUCT980, and evaluated its antibacterial activity and therapeutic potential. Transmission electron microscopy showed that BUCT980 is a myovirus. One-step growth analysis indicated an apparent latent period of approximately 60 min and a burst size of approximately 173 PFU per infected cell. The BUCT980 genome is 60,697 bp in length, and comparative genomic and phylogenetic analyses support its placement within the class. No known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes were identified by genomic analysis., BUCT980 markedly suppressed the growth ofPAO1 across the tested multiplicities of infections (MOIs) and inhibited biofilm formation. In 10-fold serial-dilution spot assays, BUCT980 formed clear plaques on 4 of 29 clinical isolates and produced visible inhibition in 13 additional isolates representing multiple sequence types. In a murine model of acutepneumonia, intranasal administration of BUCT980 significantly improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. No overt histopathological abnormalities were observed in the liver or kidney during short-term observation. These findings support further evaluation of BUCT980 as a candidate therapeutic phage for acutelung infection.IMPORTANCEis a major cause of difficult-to-treat respiratory infections because of its antibiotic resistance and biofilm-forming capacity. Here, we characterized BUCT980, a lytic phage that suppressedgrowth, inhibited early biofilm formation, and showed activity against clinical isolates from multiple sequence-type backgrounds. Genomic screening identified no known lysogeny-associated genes, virulence factors, or antibiotic resistance genes. In a murine acute pneumonia model, intranasal BUCT980 treatment improved survival, reduced pulmonary bacterial burden, and alleviated lung injury. Bacterial regrowth during prolonged exposure and limited activity against established biofilms indicate that combination strategies may be needed for sustained treatment. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of BUCT980 for acutelung infection.

title: Inhibition of Horizontal Gene Transfers under Antibiotic Stress Switches Multi-Drug Resistance to Multi-Drug Hyper-susceptibility in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
abstract: To study the effect of spatial distancing between bacteria on horizontal gene transfers, and on the evolution of multi-drug resistance and multi-drug susceptibility to antibiotics. We controlled the plating density of bacteria on agar, and showed that, by repeatedly stressing P. aeruginosa with aztreonam, spatial distancing lowers the rate of minimum inhibitory concentration increase and the number of resistant strains. More importantly, resistant PAO1 that evolved without horizontal gene transfers exhibited 2- to 64-fold increases in susceptibility as that of the wild-type PAO1 to multiple unrelated antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin, imipenem, and tetracycline, with which the bacteria were not treated a priori. While biofilm formation by the wild-type PAO1 is generally promoted by antibiotics, biofilm formation by the hypersusceptible PAO1 was inhibited by the sub-minimum inhibitory concentration of antibiotics. By spatial distancing, stressing PAO1 with aztreonam caused bacteria to become multi-drug hyper-susceptible rather than the reported multi-drug resistant. The biofilm formation by the hyper-susceptible strain was inhibited, rather than promoted, by sub-lethal concentrations of multiple antibiotics.

title: Mortality outcomes and their predictors in patients with carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii bacteraemia: a prospective cohort study from South India
journal: Trans R Soc Trop Med Hyg
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB) bloodstream infections (BSIs) are associated with high mortality, yet predictors of early mortality remain inadequately studied. We conducted a prospective observational study of patients with CRAB-BSI from July 2021 to December 2023. Patients ≥18 y of age with CRAB bacteraemia were included. Clinical, microbiological and treatment data were collected. Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of 7-d mortality. A total of 154 patients were included. The 7- and 30-d mortality rates were 57.1% and 76.6%, respectively. Common BSI sources included hospital-acquired pneumonia (51.3%) and vascular catheters (29.2%). Only 37% received appropriate empirical therapy. On multivariable analysis, type 2 diabetes mellitus (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 2.35, p=0.031), inotrope requirement at BSI onset (aOR 3.11 [95% confidence interval 1.28 to 7.56], p=0.013) and higher tigecycline minimum inhibitory concentration in Vitek-2 (aOR 2.50, p=0.040) were independent predictors of early mortality. Vascular catheter-related BSI (aOR 0.25, p=0.003) was associated with lower early mortality. The association between appropriate targeted therapy (aOR 0.21, p=0.001) and mortality was interpreted cautiously because of potential survivor bias. Early mortality in patients with CRAB-BSI is linked to host factors, severity of illness and antimicrobial resistance. Catheter-associated BSI, likely reflecting the feasibility of source control, was associated with improved outcomes. Appropriate targeted therapy was also associated with survival, which should be interpreted cautiously because of potential survivor bias.

title: Intestinal Carriage of Extended-Spectrum Cephalosporin-Resistant Enterobacterales in Farmed Sea Bream (Sparus aurata) Marketed in Algiers
abstract: This study investigated the intestinal carriage of extended-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant (ESC-R) Enterobacterales in farmed sea bream () marketed in Algiers. A total of 108 intestinal samples were collected from seven fishmongers between 2023 and 2024. ESC-R Enterobacterales were detected in 16.7% of the samples (18/108), including(= 9),(= 8), and(= 1). Whole-genome sequencing confirmed the presence of genes conferring an extended-spectrum β-lactamase phenotype in 17 isolates (mostly) and an AmpC cephalosporinase phenotype in one isolate. Moreover, theandgenes, which respectively confer resistance to colistin and fosfomycin, were detected in a singleisolate. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of plasmid-mediated colistin resistance in Algerian aquaculture. Most isolates (72.2%) exhibited a multidrug-resistant (MDR) phenotype, mainly involving resistance to tetracyclines, sulfonamide-trimethoprim, and streptomycin. Several sequence types (STs) identified in this study, including the high-risk clonesST131 andST37, have previously been reported in humans and animals. In addition, two ESC-Risolates were recovered. These findings demonstrate the occurrence of ESC-resistant bacteria in the intestinal microbiota of farmed sea bream marketed in Algiers and underscore the need for integrated One Health surveillance to better understand the role of aquaculture in the emergence, maintenance, and dissemination of MDR bacteria and antimicrobial resistance determinants.

title: Dihydromyricetin as an Antibiofilm and Antibacterial Agent Against Streptococcus agalactiae
abstract: (Group B) is a leading causative agent of sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis in neonates and is also a major pathogen responsible for bovine mastitis, posing a substantial threat to food safety and public health via the dairy production chain. The ability ofto form biofilms in the host enhances its resistance to conventional antibiotics and host immune defenses, thereby contributing to persistent and chronic infections. This study aimed to evaluate the antibacterial, antibiofilm, and combined antibacterial effects of dihydromyricetin (DMY) against thestrain GBS2 isolated from bovine mastitis. DMY exhibited significant antibacterial activity against GBS2, with a minimum inhibitory concentration and minimum bactericidal concentration of 0.5 mg/mL. Crystal violet staining and confocal laser scanning microscopy analyses demonstrated that DMY effectively inhibited and disrupted biofilm formation, resulting in looser and less dense biofilm structures compared to untreated controls. Furthermore, reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) results revealed that DMY modulated the transcript levels of biofilm-associated genes (,,,, and). Additionally, DMY markedly potentiated the antibacterial effect of penicillin G, ciprofloxacin, oxacillin, and vancomycin. These findings suggest that DMY could serve as a natural antibiofilm agent for controllingcontamination in the dairy industry, thereby contributing to the prevention of foodborne infections and reducing reliance on conventional antibiotics.

title: Bioprocessing of Talaromyces purpurogenus for production of dihydromonascorubrin with a powerful antioxidant and antimicrobial activities integrated with the network-guided target prediction and molecular docking analyses
abstract: The antibiotic resistance of pathogenic microorganisms due to the irresponsible use in healthcare and agricultural practices is one of the global threats for the human, especially immune-compromised patients. Thus, searching for a novel compounds from fungi with unique affinity to combat the drug-resistant microorganisms was the objective. Talaromyces purpurogenus # PZ292970.1, an endophyte of palm tree Elaeis guineensis, has the highest productivity of azaphilone pigment (25.5 AU410/ml), with a strong activity against E. coli (MIC value 6.8 µg/ml), S. aureus and C. albicans (MIC value 12.5 µg/ml). The extracted pigment of T. purpurogenus has a strong antibiofilm activity for S. aureus (86.2%), C. albicans (85.8%) and E. coli (79.7%), compared to the control. The TLC purified-pigment of T. purpurogenus had a maximum absorbance at λnm, with a small one at λnm, revealing the identity of the major peak as orange azaphilone pigment. The purified pigment gave a distinct single peak by HPLC, ensures their structural homogeneity. From the FT-IR analyses, the absorption and stretching vibration of the target compound functional groups ensures their spectral identity as polyketide azaphilone. The 1HNMR and 13CNMR spectra revealed characteristic proton signals for the aromatic polyketide related to dihydromonascorubrin derivatives. From LC-MS/MS, the purified compound had 385.2 m/z that were matched to the molecular mass of dihydromonascorubrin, compared the authentic dihydromonascorubrin (382.4 m/z) as suggest from the fragmentation pattern by CFM-ID software. The yield of azaphilone pigment was increased by 2 folds upon bioprocessing by Plackett-Burman design, and by 2.4 folds by γ-irradiation at 1.0 kGy. The pigment showed a powerful antioxidant activity with free radical scavenging and reducing properties as reported by DPPH, ABT and FRAP assays. Integrating target prediction and molecular docking in silico analyses, dihydromonascorubrin exhibited multi-target mechanisms linked to efflux-associated resistance in E. coli and peptidoglycan remodeling in S. aureus.

title: National trends in antimicrobial consumption in Nepal, 2016-2023: an ecological analysis
Antimicrobial resistance and documented empirical antibiotic prescribing among cancer patients with culture-confirmed infections at a tertiary referral hospital in Rwanda, 2019-2024
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens infection management in cancer patients, yet data from sub-Saharan African oncology settings are scarce. We described the microbiology, resistance patterns and documented empirical prescribing among cancer patients with culture-confirmed infection in Rwanda. We conducted a retrospective, records-based study of 297 culture-confirmed infection episodes in 286 cancer patients at King Faisal Hospital, Kigali, from 2019 to 2024. Routine susceptibility results were interpreted with the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoints in use at the time. Multidrug resistance (MDR) was classified with the organism-specific definitions of Magiorakos et al., which covered 232 of 254 bacterial isolates. Factors associated with MDR were examined by modified Poisson regression (adjusted prevalence ratios, aPR) with sensitivity analyses. Empirical regimens documented in the electronic medical record (EMR; 105 episodes, 100 inpatient) were compared with the WHO AWaRe framework and the 2022 Rwanda Standard Treatment Guidelines. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) predominated (172/297; 57.9%). Escherichia coli (101/297; 34.0%), Klebsiella spp. (32/297; 10.8%) and Enterococcus spp. (25/297; 8.4%) were the commonest isolates, and ESKAPEE pathogens accounted for 201/297 episodes (67.7%). MDR was identified in 138 of 232 covered isolates (59.5%; 95% CI 53.1-65.6) and 138 of 214 classifiable isolates (64.5%; 95% CI 57.9-70.6); restricting to more complete panels increased the estimate. Ceftriaxone resistance was high (E. coli 65/87, 74.7%; Klebsiella spp. 20/29, 69.0%), and carbapenem resistance in Acinetobacter spp. was 8/13 (61.5%). MDR prevalence did not differ by infection type (aPR versus UTI: bloodstream 0.94, 95% CI 0.67-1.31; skin and soft tissue 0.98, 95% CI 0.72-1.34) and was lower among gram-positive isolates (aPR 0.42, 95% CI 0.21-0.85), owing to Enterococcus spp. Adherence of documented regimens to the national guideline was lowest for UTIs (1/43; 2.3%). Outpatient empirical prescribing was rarely documented in the EMR and could not be evaluated. MDR was common across all infection types, and ceftriaxone, the most frequently documented empirical agent, showed limited in vitro activity against the prevailing isolates. Whether oncology-specific empirical protocols based on local antibiograms are warranted should be evaluated prospectively, including clinical outcomes, alongside AWaRe-aligned stewardship and better documentation of prescribing.

title: Emerging contaminants in hospital wastewater: A critical review of characteristics, fate, risks, and treatment
abstract: Hospital wastewater (HWW) represents a critical source of environmental and public health concerns, particularly in the post-epidemic era marked by frequent infectious disease outbreaks. This review offers a comprehensive overview of the characteristics, fate, risks, and remediation strategies of emerging contaminants (ECs) in HWW. The characteristics and properties of typical ECs reported in HWW are systematically analyzed. Six major classes of pharmaceuticals and ten classes of antibiotics have been detected. Statistical analysis reveals that iodinated contrast media (ICMs) are detected at the highest concentrations (up to 1050 μg/L), whereas antibiotics show the highest detection frequencies. The occurrence of last-resort antibiotic resistance genes (LARGs) in HWW has also been frequently reported. Analysis of environmental fate shows that ECs are probably transformed via photolysis, hydrolysis, biotransformation, adsorption, and deposition. Ecotoxicological risk assessment indicates that the LCfor sensitive organisms occurs at HWW proportions of only 0.508%-6.1% (v/v) over exposure durations of 12-96 h. Particularly, the effectiveness of advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) is evaluated in real HWW treatment. The removal rates of COD, TOC, NH-N, ARGs, and ECs (where reported) across electrochemical AOPs, photochemical AOPs, ozonation, and persulfate activation are statistically analyzed. Moreover, the performance, advantages, and limitations of various AOPs are critically compared to guide tailored HWW management. Pilot-scale devices have also been evaluated for real HWW treatment, demonstrating considerable promise for practical application. This review is expected to serve as a valuable reference for academic researchers and practicing engineers engaged in HWW treatment and environmental risk control.

title: Recent advances in the synthesis, structural diversification, and biological evaluation of sulfamethoxazole derivatives
abstract: Sulfamethoxazole is a clinically important sulfonamide antibiotic that remains a valuable pharmacophore in medicinal chemistry due to its established antibacterial activity and structural versatility. However, the emergence of antimicrobial resistance and limitations related to solubility, pharmacokinetics, and safety have encouraged extensive structural modification of the sulfamethoxazole scaffold. This review summarizes recent advances in the synthesis, structural diversification, and biological evaluation of sulfamethoxazole derivatives, with emphasis on developments reported during the last five years. Major synthetic approaches discussed include conventional sulfonamide-bond formation, greener synthetic protocols, metal complexation, Schiff base formation, nucleophilic substitution, amidation, cyanoacetylation, chloroacetylation, diazotization, heterocyclic annulation, and hybridization with other pharmacologically active scaffolds. Attention is given to how modification of the aromatic amino group, sulfonamide moiety, and isoxazole ring influences physicochemical properties and biological performance. The review also highlights sulfamethoxazole-based metal complexes, heterocyclic hybrids, prodrug-like derivatives, and nanocarrier-based systems as promising strategies to enhance antimicrobial potency and broaden biological applications, including anticancer, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, enzyme-inhibitory, and antibiofilm activities. Overall, this review provides an integrated overview of the relationship between synthetic design, structural features, and biological activity, offering useful guidance for the future development of sulfamethoxazole-based therapeutic candidates.

title: Mitochondrial iron homeostasis is required for azole tolerance in Candida albicans
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is an escalating global concern with the human fungal pathogen, Candida albicans, increasingly exhibiting resistance to fluconazole (FLC). Together with the high mortality associated with bloodstream infections, this growing resistance contributed to the classification of C. albicans as a critical priority pathogen by the World Health Organisation (WHO). Notably, C. albicans can survive high concentrations of fluconazole (FLC) through a phenomenon termed tolerance, which is different from resistance as tolerant cells grow slowly. Tolerance is considered a precursor to resistance development. Previous work from our laboratory demonstrated that intracellular iron homeostasis, particularly the mobilisation of vacuolar iron stores, modulates the synergistic interaction between doxycycline, an iron chelator, and FLC. Building on this, we hypothesised that mitochondrial iron plays a central role in determining FLC susceptibility, supported by emerging links between mitochondrial function, iron metabolism, and azole response. Mitochondrial iron import is mediated by MRS4, after which iron is primarily incorporated into iron-sulfur clusters and haem. Here, we investigated the role of mitochondrial iron import via MRS4 in azole susceptibility phenotypes, including tolerance, synergy and cidality. We demonstrate that MRS4 is essential for FLC tolerance under iron-chelating conditions, despite minimal effects on minimal inhibitory concentration or drug synergy. Absence of MRS4 results in mitochondrial dysfunction and accumulation of toxic sterol intermediates during FLC treatment. Collectively, our findings reveal that mitochondrial iron homeostasis critically governs azole tolerance and highlights toxic sterol accumulation as a driver of fungicidal outcomes.

title: Integrative metabolomics and chemometric analysis reveal metabolites associated with antibacterial and antibiofilm activities of celery, Coriander, and parsley against multidrug-resistant uropathogenic Escherichia coli
abstract: The emergence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) uropathogenic Escherichia coli and the increasing prevalence of biofilm-associated infections have created an urgent need for new antimicrobial strategies. Celery (Apium graveolens L.), coriander (Coriandrum sativum L.), and parsley (Petroselinum crispum) are widely consumed herbs with reported medicinal properties; however, the relationship between their metabolite composition and antimicrobial potential remains insufficiently understood. This study investigated whether differences in the metabolite profiles of these Apiaceae herbs are associated with their antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli isolates. Methanolic extracts of celery, coriander, and parsley, together with their derived methylene chloride: water (50:50, v/v) fractions, were evaluated for antibacterial and antibiofilm activities against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli. Untargeted LC-QTOF-MS/MS metabolomics in positive and negative ionization modes was combined with multivariate chemometric analyses to characterize metabolite profiles, discriminate among the three herbs, and identify metabolites associated with the observed biological activities. A total of 167 metabolites were annotated, including flavonoids, coumarins, phenolic acids, fatty acids, chlorins, and amino acid derivatives. Chemometric analyses clearly differentiated the three Apiaceae species based on their metabolic composition. Coriander exhibited the strongest antibacterial activity, with a minimum inhibitory concentration of 3.75 µg/mL, while all tested extracts demonstrated significant inhibition of biofilm formation. Integration of metabolomic and bioactivity data highlighted hydroxylated fatty acids, quercetin derivatives, coumarins, chlorin-related metabolites, and eucommicin A as candidate metabolites associated with antibacterial and antibiofilm effects. This study provides the first integrated metabolomics-guided comparison of celery, coriander, and parsley against clinical MDR uropathogenic E. coli isolates. By linking metabolite signatures with antibacterial and antibiofilm activities, the findings offer new insight into the phytochemical basis of the biological effects of these edible herbs and identify promising candidates for future bioassay-guided and mechanistic studies aimed at combating antimicrobial resistance and biofilm-associated infections.

title: Antimicrobial resistance and chlorhexidine susceptibility in canine staphylococcal isolates from dogs with pyoderma and clinically healthy dogs
abstract: Staphylococci, particularly Staphylococcus pseudintermedius, are the major pathogens of canine pyoderma. Meanwhile, the emergence of antimicrobial resistance has become a global concern. Chlorhexidine digluconate is widely used antiseptic in veterinary medicine; however, recent studies on chlorhexidine susceptibility in veterinary staphylococci remain limited. This study evaluated the antimicrobial resistance, chlorhexidine digluconate susceptibility, and presence of antiseptic resistance-associated genes (qacA/B, qacG, and smr) in staphylococcal isolates from dogs with pyoderma and clinically healthy dogs in Korea. In total, 145 staphylococcal isolates were obtained, including S. pseudintermedius and S. schleiferi. Antimicrobial susceptibility was evaluated using the disk diffusion. Chlorhexidine digluconate susceptibility was determined using the microdilution, qacA/B and smr were detected using real-time PCR, and qacG was detected using conventional PCR. Of the 145 isolates, 93 (64.1%) were classified as multidrug-resistant (MDR). Chlorhexidine digluconate minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) ranged from 0.25 to 2 μg/mL, with no significant difference between MDR and non-MDR isolates. qacA/B, qacG, and smr were detected in 4, 13, and 10 isolates, respectively. Isolates carrying both qacA/B and smr showed relatively higher MICs; however, the number of positive isolates was small, and single-gene carriage was not clearly associated with increased MICs. Overall, the chlorhexidine digluconate MICs were substantially lower than the clinical concentrations, and antiseptic resistance-associated genes were detected at low frequencies. Despite the high frequency of MDR isolates, chlorhexidine digluconate remains a useful antiseptic option, although continuous monitoring of reduced susceptibility and antiseptic resistance-associated genes is warranted.

title: Community context redirects evolutionary trajectories under stress
abstract: Adaptation to abiotic stress is typically studied in single-species cultures, yet bacteria inhabit and evolve in multispecies communities where neighboring organisms reshape, for example, nutrient availability, redox state, and cellular physiology. We recently demonstrated that interspecies interactions can alter the fitness effects of antibiotic resistance mutations, and we suggest that this reflects a broader principle. Stress-response networks are extensively cross-regulated and draw upon a shared, finite pool of proteomic and energetic resources. Consequently, activation of one pathway constrains others, creating physiological trade-offs. Because microbial interactions routinely perturb the physiological inputs to these networks, they can systematically redirect evolutionary trajectories under abiotic stress. We discuss the evidence, limitations, and implications of this framework for predicting evolution and understanding microbiome stability.

title: Microbial resistance from genotype to metabolic phenotype
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) poses an escalating global threat, yet surveillance and mechanistic understanding remain anchored in individual resistance genes, an approach that is inadequate for capturing the ecological, genomic, and metabolic complexity through which resistance emerges and spreads. In this opinion article, we argue that genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) offer a principled framework for advancing AMR research beyond this gene-centric paradigm. Strain-resolved GEMs embed resistance determinants within metabolic networks, with the potential to generate quantitative, context-dependent phenotypic predictions, including minimum inhibitory concentrations and environment-conditional resistance, that sequence-based tools do not provide. Expanded GEM frameworks incorporating mobile genetic elements, horizontal gene transfer, and community-level interactions support ecology-aware resistance profiling. At the therapeutic level, whole-network modelling can identify metabolic vulnerabilities, synthetic lethal interactions, and microbiome-targeted strategies. Integrating GEMs with multiomics and data-driven approaches represents a critical step toward a mechanism-aware AMR platform connecting surveillance, diagnosis, and drug discovery.

title: Supersulfides in bacterial antibiotic resistance: chemical inactivation, redox signaling, and translational opportunities
abstract: The global spread of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria has emerged as one of the most pressing public health challenges worldwide. Because the development of novel antibiotics remains slow and increasingly difficult, innovative therapeutic strategies are urgently needed. Supersulfides, including persulfides and polysulfides, are ubiquitous sulfur species found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes. Owing to their exceptional nucleophilicity and antioxidant capacity, they play central roles in cellular redox signaling and stress adaptation. Recent studies have further revealed that bacterial supersulfides contribute to antibiotic resistance through multiple mechanisms, including the direct chemical inactivation of β-lactam antibiotics, activation of multidrug efflux pumps, and detoxification of reactive oxygen species generated during antibiotic treatment. These findings identify bacterial supersulfide biosynthetic pathways as promising targets for the development of next-generation antimicrobial therapies. In this Review, we summarize current knowledge of supersulfide biosynthesis, with particular emphasis on recently identified pathways unique to bacteria. We also discuss the diverse mechanisms by which bacterial supersulfides promote antibiotic resistance and highlight recent advances in pharmacological strategies targeting supersulfide biosynthesis. Finally, we discuss the translational potential of targeting bacterial supersulfide metabolism and the key challenges that must be overcome for clinical application.

title: Does transfusion of blood products increase the risk of multidrug-resistant infections in critically ill patients?
abstract: To investigate the association between transfusion of blood products during intensive care unit (ICU) stay and the incidence of ICU-acquired colonisation and infection with multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria (ICU-MDR-col, ICU-MDR-inf, respectively). Secondary analysis of two prospective multicentre cohort studies conducted in eight ICUs in France. Adult patients admitted to participating ICUs were enrolled consecutively from May 2019 to June 2021. All patients underwent systematic screening for colonisation with MDR bacteria at admission and weekly thereafter. Exposure to transfusion of blood products during ICU stay, including packed red blood cells (PRBCs), fresh frozen plasma (FFP) and platelet concentrates (PCs), was recorded. The primary outcome was the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and/or ICU-MDR-inf (ICU-MDR-col/inf) until ICU discharge, censored at day 28. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of ICU-MDR-col and ICU-MDR-inf, considered separately. Associations were assessed using mixed-effects Poisson regression models adjusted for prespecified confounders. Subgroup analyses were performed according to immunosuppression status at ICU admission. Among 1103 patients, 358 (32.5%) received transfusion of any blood product. Overall, 292 (26.5%) patients experienced at least one ICU-MDR-col/inf event. Transfusion was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-MDR-col/inf (adjusted incidence rate ratio [aIRR] 1.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.06-1.62; p = 0.013), mainly driven by ICU-MDR-inf (aIRR 1.62, 95% CI 1.16-2.24; p = 0.004), but not ICU-MDR-col considered individually. This association was restricted to PRBC transfusion. No significant heterogeneity was observed according to immunosuppression status. Transfusion of PBRCs was associated with an increased incidence of ICU-acquired MDR infections, with no significant heterogeneity observed according to immunosuppression status. These findings support a restrictive approach to transfusion and warrant further investigation into its immunological and ecological consequences in critically ill patients.

title: Emergence of Candida (Candidozyma) auris in Warming Climates
abstract: ()is a pathogenic fungus first identified in a patient in 2009. Prior to this clinical finding,was unknown, with its closest relative being the marine-dwellingInfections are increasing annually, predominately impacting hospital patients due to durable biofilms on medical devices and antimicrobial resistance. Perplexingly, the fungus arose nearly simultaneously across the globe in independent disease emergences from six genetically distinct clades. Theclades mostly diverged from one another 5,000-10,000 years ago, during a period when global temperatures and sea levels rose and coastal wetlands flourished. Within the past 200-300 years, a new wave of rapid divergence occurred within each clade. This corresponds to industrialization, urbanization, global warming, and the widespread wetland destruction. Environmental stressors, including heat, are hypothesized to have driven mutations and stress resistance. These may not only helpwithstand a changing climate but also help it thrive within mammalian hosts.

title: How do we monitor doxy-PEP impact and when should we consider revisiting guidelines?
abstract: The 2026 WHO guidelines recommending doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxy-PEP) represent the first global antibiotic prophylaxis recommendation for bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with provisions for antimicrobial resistance (AMR) monitoring.Doxy-PEP should be governed as an adaptive intervention subject to periodic, transparent review, but establishing decision rules faces challenges.Doxy-PEP is expected to select for resistance, including in Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Staphylococcus aureus, and the gut and skin microbiomes; the scope of clinical consequences is incompletely understood.As STI prevalence falls, the benefit per dose declines while the AMR externality per dose is expected to grow, shifting the cost-benefit balance in ways that vary across populations and settings.Attributing changes in disease prevalence or resistance patterns to doxy-PEP is methodologically difficult, given incompletely understood and complex drivers of pre-existing trends, surveillance limitations, and heterogeneous uptake, raising questions about study designs, data sources, eligibility criteria, and governance mechanisms.A full accounting of benefits and harms is broader than reduced bacterial STI incidence and AMR. Benefits include consideration of patient-centered outcomes such as reduced anxiety regarding STI acquisition, avoidance of repeated treatment visits, and fewer STI-related complications. Harms include drug side effects, such as gastrointestinal adverse effects and concerns about use in pregnancy.

title: Analysis of the impact of naturally-acquired immunity on Shigella vaccine performance to inform clinical trials: A simulation-based modeling study
abstract: Effective vaccines against Shigella, the leading bacterial cause of diarrheal disease globally, could prevent morbidity and mortality from shigellosis as well as limit antibiotic resistance. Several Shigella vaccine candidates are in late stages of development, and the design of large Phase 3 trials in target populations is underway. In high incidence settings, children are expected to rapidly accrue natural immunity such that after repeated pathogen exposure, unvaccinated infants may have similar levels of immunity as vaccinated infants. For this reason, in these settings estimates of vaccine efficacy (VE) may underestimate expected efficacy in a fully naïve population. To set expectations and support optimal planning of future Shigella vaccine trials, we aimed to quantify the potential impact of this phenomenon on VE estimates under different surveillance strategies and assumptions about Shigella immunity. We simulated Shigella vaccine trials in low-, medium-, and high-burden settings under different assumptions about vaccine- and infection-conferred immunity. We estimated VE against severe, Shigella-attributable disease and any Shigella-attributable diarrhea under six trial designs: active surveillance for Shigella infection or symptom-based reporting paired with single-outcome, stratified recurrent outcome, or crude recurrent-outcome Cox proportional hazards models. In each scenario, we evaluated bias, 95% confidence interval (CI) coverage, and the false negative rate. Only the trial design using active surveillance for infection and single outcome models was consistently unbiased across all examined scenarios. The other five designs underestimated VE by up to an absolute 20%, with a single outcome model paired with symptom-based reporting performing least poorly. Bias generally was worse at higher-burden sites. For realistically sized trials, the 95% CI coverage and false negative rate were also worse at higher-burden sites. The results were sensitive to input parameters which depended on assumptions about Shigella natural history based on limited published data. The observed VE in Shigella vaccine trials is likely to underestimate true VE, though the magnitude of underestimation described here is conditional on the simulation's inputs and assumptions. Careful trial design is needed to minimize this underestimation.

title: Genomic Exploration of CRISPR-Cas Systems in Raoultella species: Diversity and Architecture
abstract: Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein (CRISPR-Cas) systems are adaptive immune mechanisms that protect bacteria against invading mobile genetic elements. They can influence horizontal gene transfer, phage resistance, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics. Although these systems have been investigated in several Klebsiella species, information on historically defined Raoultella species remains limited. In this study, 103 complete genomes representing Raoultella species, currently placed within the broader Klebsiella lineage, were analyzed to characterize the distribution, architecture, and diversity of CRISPR-Cas systems. CRISPR-Cas loci were identified using CRISPRCasFinder and CRISPRone, followed by subtype classification, direct repeat and leader sequence analyses, spacer matching, Cas1-based phylogenetic analysis, and AMR determinant screening. Complete CRISPR-Cas systems were detected in 23 genomes, predominantly in R. ornithinolytica strains. All complete systems were chromosomally located, whereas plasmid-associated orphan CRISPR arrays were observed in selected R. ornithinolytica strains. Two major architectures were identified, with Type I-E being dominant and Type I-F restricted to fewer strains. Direct repeat analysis revealed six consensus sequences, while leader regions displayed conserved AT-rich motifs and strain-specific divergence. Spacer analyses suggested historical interactions with phages and plasmids, particularly mobile genetic elements associated with Klebsiella and other Enterobacteriaceae. Cas1 phylogeny showed subtype-dependent clustering, indicating that CRISPR-Cas evolution does not strictly follow core genome phylogeny. The coexistence of predicted CRISPR-Cas loci and AMR determinants indicates that the presence of these loci does not necessarily preclude the carriage of resistance determinants. Overall, this study expands current knowledge of CRISPR-Cas diversity among the analyzed Raoultella genomes and provides a genomic framework for future functional studies.

title: Expanding threat of carbapenemase-producing Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae in Peru: genomic and phenotypic evidence of high-risk clones dissemination
abstract: Carbapenemase-producingrepresent a growing global threat due to their extensive antimicrobial resistance and rapid dissemination. This study characterized the phenotypic and genomic features ofandisolates collected between 2020 and 2022 from four healthcare institutions in Lima, Peru. A total of 320 non-redundant isolates (61and 259) were analyzed through antimicrobial susceptibility testing, polymerase chain reaction, and whole-genome sequencing. The most frequent carbapenemase gene was(69%), followed by(16.9%) and(4.6%). Elevenisolates co-produced NDM and KPC, and oneisolate co-harbored NDM and OXA-48-like. All isolates were multidrug-resistant, and 5% were resistant to all agents included in the routine panel; however, aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol retained completeactivity among tested isolates. Novel β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor combinations such as aztreonam/avibactam and cefiderocol showed complete activity against all classes of carbapenemases. Genomic analysis revealed predominantsequence types ST167 and ST410 andlineages ST147, ST15, ST45, and ST273. Theallele was detected for the first time in Peru, mostly in, and was carried on multireplicon IncF-type plasmids. In, ST147 was identified as a dominant clone associated with, indicating sustained local dissemination of high-risk clonal groups. The coexistence of multiple carbapenemases and plasmid backbones highlights the ongoing evolution of resistance mechanisms. This work provides the first integrative genomic overview of carbapenemase-producingandin Peru and underscores the need for continuous genomic surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship to mitigate their clinical and epidemiological impact.

title: Purification and mechanistic characterisation of bacillomycin D homologues from Bacillus velezensis PD9 with antibiofilm activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance continues to undermine treatment of multidrug-resistant infections, necessitating new antimicrobial agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Bacillus velezensis PD9 (BvPD9), isolated from Heterotrigona itama propolis, produces antibacterial lipopeptides; however, the active bacillomycin D homologues and their mechanisms remain insufficiently characterised. Here, an optimised extraction and chromatographic purification workflow was developed, enabling selective enrichment of two bioactive fractions putatively assigned by LC-TOF-MS/MS as C14-enriched bacillomycin D and a C14/C15-bacillomycin D homologue mixture. The C14-enriched bacillomycin D fraction exhibited selective activity against Staphylococcus spp. and vancomycin-sensitive Enterococcus faecium (VSEF), with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of 16-32 µg/mL, whereas the C14/C15 homologue mixture demonstrated broader antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and selected ESKAPE pathogens (Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter spp.) (MICs 16-512 µg/mL), with the lowest MIC (16 µg/mL) observed against VSEF. Both compounds retained activity following heat exposure (40-80 °C), wide pH variation (4-12), and proteolytic enzymes. The C14/C15 homologue mixture was prioritised for further evaluation because of its broader antibacterial spectrum and displayed concentration-dependent inhibition of biofilm formation, membrane permeabilisation, and ultrastructural alterations, together with changes in bacterial DNA-content distribution without detectable direct DNA binding. Preliminary safety evaluation demonstrated concentration-dependent haemolysis and cytotoxicity at higher concentrations, while zebrafish embryos showed concentration-dependent mortality with an LCof 109.54 µg/mL at 120 hpf. Serial passaging resulted in a four-fold MIC increase only during the final passages, whereas chloramphenicol showed no detectable MIC change under the same conditions. Overall, the findings demonstrate antibacterial and membrane-associated activities of PD9-derived bacillomycin D-enriched fractions and provide a basis for further investigation of individually purified homologues.

title: Meeting gene expression demand during evolution of antibiotic resistance
abstract: Regulated gene expression in bacteria accommodates demands imposed by different environments. In addition to ensuring the production of required metabolic and structural components, gene regulation protects bacteria against the adverse effects of misexpression. Upon encountering a novel environment, such as sustained exposure to antibiotics, transcriptional recalibration ensues to improve fitness. For antibiotics, this involves enhancing the expression of an existing repertoire of resistance mechanisms and is often mediated by mutations in regulators of gene expression. Here, we review how diverse gene regulatory mutations confer antibiotic resistance to bacterial pathogens. We view these strategies through the lens of the Gene Expression Demand Theory, originally proposed for inducible operons involved in sugar metabolism, and describe the molecular basis and evolutionary consequences for a few well-studied examples. Broad underlying preferences of when and which kind of regulatory mutations bacteria employ emerge from these examples. A key pattern appears to be a preference for derepression rather than activating mutations, and we highlight potential underlying genetic and evolutionary explanations. Finally, even as our knowledge of molecular mechanisms of antibiotic adaptation continues to expand, we propose that adaptation by regulatory mutations provides a framework for assessing the risk of resistance evolution in the case of novel antibiotics and alternative targets for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions.

title: Physicochemical characterization of a bioactive Minthostachys verticillata nanoemulsion with enhanced antibacterial efficacy against veterinary pathogens
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance among livestock pathogens represents a growing challenge for veterinary medicine, underscoring the need for effective plant-based alternatives. This study describes the development and physicochemical characterization of an oil-in-water nanoemulsion incorporatingessential oil (EO) and evaluates its biocompatibility and antibacterial efficacy. The EO, obtained by steam distillation (yield 4.8% v/w), was chemically characterized by GC-MS, revealing a pulegone-menthone chemotype. A series of nanoemulsion formulations were prepared by modulating surfactant composition and processing parameters, leading to the selection of an optimized formulation (NE2-S). This nanoemulsion exhibited a mean droplet size of 103.2 nm, low polydispersity (PDI = 0.279), and moderate electrostatic stabilization, complemented by steric stabilization provided by non-ionic surfactants (ζ-potential = -22.5 mV). Biocompatibility assessment using an MTT assay in murine fibroblasts demonstrated low cytotoxicity at concentrations up to 2500 μg/mL. Antibacterial evaluation against enterotoxigenic(ETEC) andrevealed enhanced efficacy of NE2-S compared with EO, with two-fold reductions in both minimum inhibitory and bactericidal concentrations. Biofilm inhibition and eradication assays were additionally performed against the same field isolates. NE2-S showed a clear advantage over EO in inhibiting and eradicating ETEC F4+ biofilm, whereas its effect againstbiofilm was more limited, with EO proving superior at eradicating pre-formedbiofilm. Overall, these findings establish a physicochemical framework linking nanoscale colloidal architecture to improved antibacterial performance, supporting the potential of this nanoemulsion platform as a promising antimicrobial strategy for the control of bacterial infections of veterinary relevance in livestock production.

title: Travel-associated Staphylococcus aureus infections: a global perspective from the GeoSentinel Surveillance Network
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, and Staphylococcus aureus is among the leading contributors to the global AMR-attributable disease burden. Data on the clinical presentation and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns of Staphylococcus aureus infections in returning travellers remain scarce. We described the clinical presentation, travel characteristics, and antimicrobial susceptibility of travellers and migrants diagnosed with Staphylococcus aureus infection through the GeoSentinel network between January 2014 and December 2022. Because no consensus definition exists for travel-associated infections, we included all cases recorded in the GeoSentinel database as travel-associated. We evaluated patients during travel or after return. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) was performed according to routine laboratory practice at participating sites. We retrieved 740 travellers and migrants with Staphylococcus aureus infection diagnosed at 50 GeoSentinel sites. Four hundred thirty-eight (59.2%) were male, and the median age was 32 years (IQR 23-48). The most frequently visited regions were Southeast Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and South-Central Asia. Most patients presented after travel (576/740; 77.8%). Skin and soft tissue infections were the predominant diagnosis (670/740; 90.5%), and most patients were managed as outpatients (579/740; 78.2%). Overall, 406/740 (54.9%) isolates showed resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class, including methicillin (224/656; 34.1%), lincosamides (144/627; 23.0%), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (129/597; 21.6%). Demographic characteristics and hospitalization frequency were similar between patients with MSSA and MRSA infections. Most Staphylococcus aureus infections in international travellers presented as skin and soft tissue infections and were managed in outpatient settings. Resistance or reduced susceptibility to at least one antimicrobial class was common, with one-third of isolates identified as methicillin-resistant. These findings support the importance of AST to guide management of skin and soft tissue infections in internationally mobile populations and reinforce the need for standardized definitions of travel-associated bacterial infections and continued global surveillance.

title: Solving the Staphylococcus aureus puzzle: lessons to guide future MRSA vaccine development
abstract: SUMMARYThe broad-spectrum use of antibiotics allows for the development of resistance in symptomatically and asymptomatically carried pathogenic bacteria. Antibiotic-resistant bacteria, with this review focusing on, cause significant morbidity and mortality and put considerable strain on the global healthcare system. In a vaccinated individual, bacteria are less likely to develop resistance mechanisms compared to an individual treated with antibiotics, highlighting a potential method for conserving antibiotic use. However, despite over a century of research, avaccine candidate is yet to progress past phase III clinical trials, and to develop a successfulvaccine, the shortcomings of previous attempts require critical analysis. After consideration of the five most successfulvaccine programs, it is identified in this review that future attempts should (i) be polyvalent to circumvent immune evasion, (ii) include carefully chosen antigens to avoid maladaptive memory, (iii) include T cell targeting to provide a comprehensive immune response, (iv) utilize multiple measures of preclinical efficacy in pre-exposed models, and (v) implement considered clinical study design, including appropriate vaccine formulation for the target population. By combining these attributes, such as in the form of epitope-based or nanoparticle vaccines, there is a promising future for the development ofvaccines that circumvent the issues that caused the downfall of previous vaccine programs, thereby protecting the global population from development toward a future where bacteria are resistant to all antibiotic treatments.

title: Wildlife-associated ecosystems in Algeria harbor internationally distributed ESBL-producing clones and plasmids, including a CTX-M-15 Klebsiella pneumoniae ST17 lineage associated with a conserved IncFIB(K) resistance plasmid
abstract: Expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales (ESC-R-E) have disseminated beyond clinical settings, but their occurrence and genomic epidemiology in wildlife remain poorly characterized, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. ESC-R may result from the production of extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBLs) or AmpC-type cephalosporinases. We investigated the prevalence, resistance mechanisms, and population structure of ESC-R-E in free-ranging wildlife, captive wild animals, and zoo workers in Algeria. Between October 2021 and June 2023, 1,899 fecal samples were collected across six Algerian provinces. ESC-R-E isolates were recovered by selective culture and characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing. Overall, 73 ESC-R-E isolates (3.9%) were identified, including seven OXA-48-like carbapenemase co-producers (0.4%). Carriage was significantly higher in captive animals (13.5%) than in free-ranging wildlife (1.6%) or zoo workers (7.7%). Among the 66 ESBL-producing isolates analyzed, CTX-M enzymes predominated (= 61), particularly CTX-M-15 (= 53).was the predominant species (= 33), with ST17 accounting for 27/33 isolates. Closely related CTX-M-15-producing ST17 isolates were recovered from captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and a zoo worker and carried an IncFIB(K) plasmid harboringwithin a multidrug resistance region closely related to globally disseminated plasmids. Globally disseminated high-riskclones were also detected, namely ST167, ST361, ST410, and a persistent ST38 lineage in Algerian wildlife since 2016. These findings demonstrate the circulation of high-risk Enterobacterales lineages and mobile resistance plasmids in Algerian wildlife-associated ecosystems and highlight the need for integrated One Health surveillance of antimicrobial resistance at the human-animal-environment interface. Wildlife is increasingly recognized as a potential reservoir and sentinel for antimicrobial resistance, yet genomic data from low- and middle-income countries remain scarce. This study provides one of the largest genomic investigations of expanded-spectrum cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales in wildlife from North Africa. We demonstrate that internationally disseminated high-riskandlineages, together with globally distributed CTX-M-15-carrying plasmids, are circulating among captive animals, free-ranging wildlife, and humans in zoological environments. The recovery of closely relatedST17 isolates from different host species highlights the potential for antimicrobial resistance dissemination across the human-animal-environment interface. These findings extend the known ecological range of clinically important resistant Enterobacterales beyond healthcare settings and identify wildlife-associated ecosystems as part of the broader antimicrobial resistance network. Our study underscores the value of integrating wildlife into One Health surveillance programs to better understand and mitigate the environmental spread of antimicrobial resistance.

title: Antidepressant desvenlafaxine identified in wastewater promotes transformation and antibiotic resistance risk in Acinetobacter baylyi ADP1 via metabolic adaptations
abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are known reservoirs of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Non-antibiotic compounds, such as antidepressants, may further promote ARG acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Desvenlafaxine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) listed on the EU Surface Water Watch List, is among the most frequently detected antidepressants in WWTP effluents, yet its role in HGT has not been examined. Here, we detected desvenlafaxine at the highest concentrations among four antidepressants monitored across three municipal WWTPs in western New York. UsingADP1 as a model recipient in natural transformation assays (= 6), we found that desvenlafaxine significantly increased transformation frequency at 10 mg/L (1.74 ± 0.33-fold) and 50 mg/L (1.49 ± 0.19-fold;< 0.05). Effects occurred without induction of reactive oxygen species or loss of membrane integrity, consistent with its very low toxicity (IC~1,300 mg/L). Instead, desvenlafaxine induced dose-dependent increases in membrane fluidity and shifts to less negative zeta potentials, suggesting that electrostatic interactions between its cationic amine group and the negatively charged membrane reduce surface repulsion and facilitate plasmid proximity during uptake. Non-targeted proteomics revealed a biphasic response: at 10 mg/L, competence-associated proteins (PilB, ComM) were upregulated, and STRING analysis identified networks linked to membrane transport, transcriptional regulation, and envelope remodeling, while no connected network was recovered at 50 mg/L. Electron microscopy confirmed higher pilus frequency at both doses. Together, these findings reveal a non-oxidative, envelope-mediated route by which a widely detected antidepressant increases bacterial competence.IMPORTANCEThe spread of antibiotic resistance poses a serious and escalating threat to human health worldwide. While antibiotic use is widely recognized as a key driver, non-antibiotic pharmaceuticals released into the environment through wastewater have received far less attention. Antidepressants are among the most frequently detected drugs in treated wastewater effluents, yet their potential to promote antibiotic resistance transfer in bacteria remains poorly understood. This study demonstrates that desvenlafaxine, one of the most abundant antidepressants found in municipal wastewater, can increase the uptake of antibiotic resistance genes in an environmental bacterium at concentrations above those currently measured in effluent, and identifies the bacterial cell-surface changes that enable this without cytotoxicity.

title: Exploring antimicrobial resistance in wild and domestic animal populations: combining publicly available data with BV-BRC resources to introduce bioinformatics in an undergraduate classroom
abstract: Bioinformatics blends the fields of biology, statistics, computer science, and information technology for the processing and analysis of genomic data. Despite the growing demand for trained bioinformaticians and a positive job market outlook, most undergraduate institutions struggle to integrate bioinformatics into their life science curricula. Educators face numerous barriers to incorporating bioinformatics into their classes, including technical issues and expertise. To address this need, we are developing web-accessible, course-based materials for general microbiology, infectious disease, genomics, and other similar undergraduate and graduate classes that use bioinformatic workflows within the Bacterial and Viral Bioinformatics Resource Center (BV-BRC), one of three National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)-funded Bioinformatics Resource Centers. Here, we present one such activity: a three-part exercise focused on antimicrobial resistance and metagenomics that uses six publicly available metagenomic samples collected from wild and domestic animal populations to explore the distinctions between their gut microbiomes and their respective antibiotic resistance genes. To analyze community composition and identify antibiotic resistance genes, students use two end-to-end services offered by the BV-BRC: Taxonomic Classification and Metagenomic Read Mapping. This assignment was developed to introduce students to core competencies in the field of bioinformatics and to highlight the BV-BRC as an educational resource for integrating bioinformatics without requiring students and instructors to possess the technical proficiencies and computing resources traditionally needed. We successfully implemented this exercise in an upper-level undergraduate microbiology course, demonstrating the feasibility of using the BV-BRC for bioinformatics education in the classroom.

title: Differential impacts of early, extended-spectrum, and last-resort β-lactams on manure-derived microbiomes and resistomes in an in vitro model
abstract: Understanding the environmental dissemination of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is crucial for mitigating its spread and reducing the clinical burden of resistant infections. In a previous study, we demonstrated that copiotrophic enrichment in a medium that stimulates the growth of gut-associated bacteria can reveal clinically associated bacterial populations and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) that are not detected through direct environmental sampling.
